# Thresholds, complexity, and hardware benchmarks {#sec-benchmarking}

## The question behind a benchmark

A decoder is useful if it helps an encoded computation meet an error budget within available classical and quantum resources. A small logical error rate is necessary, but a comparison is incomplete without the code, circuit, noise process, runtime, and definition of failure. This chapter turns that observation into a quantitative evaluation method.

The central observable for a fixed memory experiment is a Bernoulli random variable $F$: one if the inferred logical observable differs from the true one, zero otherwise. Its mean $p_L$ is a logical failure probability for that experiment. A full Pauli-memory test may track both logical components. A computational-basis memory test can miss logical phase errors. A multi-logical-qubit code introduces another distinction: failure of any logical qubit versus average per-qubit failure.

## Failure per experiment and per round

Suppose an independent logical parity flip occurs each round with probability $\epsilon$. After $T$ rounds, an odd number of flips produces a final error, so

$$
P_T=\sum_{j\text{ odd}}\binom Tj\epsilon^j(1-\epsilon)^{T-j}
=\frac{1-(1-2\epsilon)^T}{2}.
$$ {#eq-bench-round}

The second equality follows by subtracting the even and odd terms in $(1-\epsilon+\epsilon)^T$ and $(1-\epsilon-\epsilon)^T$. Inverting gives

$$
\epsilon=\frac{1-(1-2P_T)^{1/T}}{2}.
$$

The approximation $P_T/T\approx\epsilon$ is valid only when $T\epsilon\ll1$. A final parity error saturates at one half; it is not the probability that at least one logical fault occurred. Initialization and readout contributions often motivate a contrast model $P_T=[1-A(1-2\epsilon)^T]/2$ with fitted $A$. Correlated faults or time-varying rates can invalidate a single exponential. Report the model and the raw round dependence.

## Finite-size scaling and its limits {#sec-finite-size-analysis}

For a fixed code family, decoder, and noise model, a decoding threshold is a physical parameter below which increasing size suppresses logical error asymptotically under the chosen scaling of experiment duration. A common surface-memory choice is $T\propto d$. A code-capacity threshold uses a different experiment. A pseudo-threshold solves $p_L(d,p)=p$ for a particular finite device and definition of $p$.

Near a continuous transition, a numerical scaling ansatz is

$$
p_L(d,p)\simeq f\big((p-p_{\mathrm{th}})d^{1/\nu}\big)
+d^{-\omega}g\big((p-p_{\mathrm{th}})d^{1/\nu}\big).
$$ {#eq-bench-scaling}

Here $\nu$ governs a diverging correlation length and $\omega>0$ parameterizes finite-size corrections. The expression is an ansatz whose quality must be checked, not a theorem for every decoder. A polynomial approximation to $f$ makes fitting practical but introduces model and fit-window choices. Good practice varies the smallest included distance, the physical-noise window, and correction terms, then reports stability. A visually attractive crossing of three small distances is preliminary evidence.

Far below threshold, one often observes

$$
p_L\approx A(d,T)\left(\frac{p}{p_0}\right)^{(d+1)/2}
$$

for odd-distance codes dominated by minimum malignant sets. The exponent assumes distance is preserved by the circuit and decoder and faults scale independently enough for the counting argument. Correlated faults, biased channels, or different boundaries can change it. Neither this empirical form nor a threshold crossing determines performance at an arbitrarily small target error without a validated extrapolation.

Error bars are 95% Wilson intervals. The small distance range illustrates suppression and crossings; it is not a precision threshold estimate.](figs/surface-memory){#fig-surface-benchmark}

The raw values, seeds, package versions, and batch decoding times behind @fig-surface-benchmark are in [surface-memory.csv](data/surface-memory.csv). This model applies noise at every named location, so its parameter should not be compared directly with a model containing only two-qubit-gate noise. Distances three, five, and seven show a crossing region near the middle of the sampled grid; the experiment deliberately does not report a fitted universal threshold.

## Statistical uncertainty and rare failures

For $K$ failures in $N$ independent trials, the likelihood is $\binom NKp_L^K(1-p_L)^{N-K}$. The maximum-likelihood estimate is $\hat p=K/N$. The normal approximation $\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/N}$ fails particularly badly when $K=0$. A Wilson interval uses $z\simeq1.96$ for an approximate 95% interval:

$$
c=\frac{\hat p+z^2/(2N)}{1+z^2/N},\qquad
r=\frac{z}{1+z^2/N}\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{N}+\frac{z^2}{4N^2}}.
$$ {#eq-bench-wilson}

Report $[c-r,c+r]$ with the counts. For zero failures, a one-sided 95% binomial upper bound is $1-0.05^{1/N}\approx3/N$. Zero observed failures is therefore compatible with a nonzero rate.

To estimate a rare rate with relative standard error about $r$, the Bernoulli approximation requires $N\approx1/(p_Lr^2)$. At $p_L=10^{-8}$ and $r=0.1$, that is roughly $10^{10}$ shots. A neural decoder that is expensive to sample or evaluate can make this validation prohibitive. Importance sampling can oversample dangerous configurations and reweight them, but the proposal must have support wherever the target has support. If samples $e_i$ come from $q(e)$, an unbiased estimator is

$$
\hat p_L=\frac1N\sum_i \frac{P(e_i)}{q(e_i)}\mathbf1\{F(e_i)=1\}.
$$

Variance can still be enormous if the proposal misses important failure mechanisms. Estimate and report it. Do not treat self-normalized weights or a learned generator's uncalibrated probabilities as an exact oracle.

For comparing two decoders, using the same test faults is valuable. Let $n_{10}$ count failures of A only and $n_{01}$ failures of B only. These discordant cases contain the evidence about their difference; independent error bars ignore the covariance. Keep a locked, independent evaluation set, especially when many architectures and hyperparameters were selected.

## Complexity is more than a big-O label

Let $n$ be data qubits, $m$ check nodes per round, $T$ rounds, and $E$ graph edges. Sparse BP uses work proportional to $E$ per iteration; its total cost includes the iteration count and postprocessing. OSD adds elimination and a candidate search whose cost grows with search order. A tensor network can have modest local tensors yet exponential exact contraction cost in a lattice width or treewidth. A truncated bond dimension changes both cost and accuracy. A Transformer attending globally to $N=mT$ tokens stores an $N\times N$ attention pattern in its straightforward implementation. Local or sparse attention changes that pattern and the information propagation depth.

| Decoder family | Useful computational unit | Scaling issue to measure |
|---|---|---|
| MWPM / sparse blossom | Detector graph and explored matching regions | Event density, difficult tails, graph construction and updates |
| Union-find | Cluster growth and peeling | Weighted variants, fault-model fidelity, logical accuracy |
| BP + OSD/LSD | Sparse message sweep plus repair | Iteration tails, elimination, cluster sizes, OSD order |
| Tensor network | Tensor contraction at bond dimension $\chi$ | Width, $\chi$ convergence, truncation bias |
| CNN / recurrent network | Local layer or recurrent update | Depth, receptive field, sequential critical path |
| GNN | Edge messages per layer | Graph communication, number of layers, consistency repair |
| Transformer | Attention and token-state update | Window size, activation memory, batch size, accelerator utilization |
| Autoregressive / diffusion | Sequential conditional or denoising step | Number of steps/samples, posterior calibration, legal output rate |

The table gives measurement targets, not a universal speed ranking. Algorithmic complexity, average CPU time, GPU throughput, and integrated feedback latency answer different questions.

## Real time: throughput, latency, and tails {#sec-real-time}

If each syndrome round arrives every $\tau_c$, the sustained service rate must keep up with that stream. A decoder may have a long pipeline but emit one result each cycle. **Throughput** measures the acceptance or completion rate; **latency** measures the elapsed time from relevant input availability to a usable result. End-to-end latency includes acquisition, transfer, preprocessing, inference, correction repair, output transfer, and controller action. Queueing and rare difficult syndromes matter even when the mean is small.

A simple work-conserving queue has waiting-time recursion

$$
W_{t+1}=\max\{0,W_t+S_t-\tau_c\},
$$ {#eq-bench-queue}

where $S_t$ is service time. A necessary average-rate condition is $\mathbb E[S_t]<\tau_c$ for the usual stationary queue assumptions; it does not by itself guarantee a small tail probability. Report median, high percentiles, worst observed latency, and the workload that generated them. Accelerator benchmarks must state batch size, warm-up, compilation, precision, and whether data-transfer time is included. A large batch can improve shots per second while making a single-shot feedback deadline worse.

The Willow surface-memory experiment is an instructive published example: its distance-five real-time decoder had an average latency of about $63\,\mu$s with a $1.1\,\mu$s cycle, while sustaining long memory streams [@GoogleWillow2025]. This is compatible with real-time throughput and a nonzero pipeline latency. The reported high-accuracy offline neural result is a separate operating point. It should not be substituted for the integrated real-time result.

## Experimental evidence across platforms

Below-threshold surface memory, logical gates, low-overhead code proposals, and autonomous calibration are complementary milestones. They test different parts of the eventual computer. The 2025 colour-code experiment by Lacroix and collaborators combined scaling and logical operations on a superconducting processor [@LacroixEtAl2025]. Bluvstein and collaborators' neutral-atom architecture studied error correction, logical operations, and physical error removal in reconfigurable arrays [@BluvsteinEtAl2026]. Their performance figures require the specified circuits, accepted runs, bases, and noise conditions; no single published number ranks all architectures.

Postselection deserves particular care. If a procedure retains a fraction $a$ of shots and has conditional error $p_{L|\mathrm{accept}}$, both quantities are necessary. For a protocol requiring $G$ independently accepted stages with no recycling, yield would scale as $a^G$; realistic recycling changes the resource calculation. A tiny conditional error with tiny acceptance is not the same resource as deterministic correction. Leakage heralding, error detection, and learned confidence filtering should be described as their actual protocols.

## A reproducible decoder comparison

A useful benchmark record includes the complete code matrices or measurement circuit; physical noise parameters and units; simulator version and seeds; detector and logical-observable conventions; training distribution and training cost; decoder configuration; independent test counts; uncertainty; consistency failures; runtime hardware and timing boundaries; and all acceptance rules. For a learned model, release the weights or a deterministic training recipe and identify calibration data used from the device. Training on test-device records can be appropriate for adaptation, but the evaluation split must make the scientific claim clear.

For every claimed gain, perform an ablation matched to its mechanism. If soft readout is added, give a classical decoder the same soft information where possible. If $X/Z$ correlations are used, compare against a correlation-aware baseline. If fine-tuning on device data helps, distinguish that gain from architectural improvements. If the output needs an exact syndrome repair stage, include its failures and latency in the result.

## Exercises and worked solutions

### Exercise 1: Interpreting no failures

A decoder has zero failures in one million independent shots. Can the paper claim $p_L<10^{-8}$ at 95% confidence?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

No. The one-sided upper bound is about $3\times10^{-6}$. To put a zero-failure 95% upper bound at $10^{-8}$ requires about $3\times10^8$ independent shots under the same conditions. Correlations can reduce the effective sample size further.
:::

### Exercise 2: Per-round normalization

A 100-round parity memory fails with probability 0.1. Under the independent identical logical-flip model, estimate the per-round error and compare with division by 100.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

$\epsilon=[1-0.8^{1/100}]/2\simeq0.0011145$, while $P_T/T=0.001$. Division underestimates the rate because an even number of flips cancels in final parity. Whether the independent model is physically justified is a separate question.
:::

### Exercise 3: Attention memory

A global attention layer has $10^4$ detector tokens and eight heads. How much storage do the attention weights alone use at two bytes per entry? Why can a local window help?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

$8(10^4)^2(2)=1.6\times10^9$ bytes, about 1.6 GB, before other activations, parameters, and gradients. A fixed neighborhood of $w$ keys per token reduces explicit weights to $O(Nw)$, but long-distance information then needs more layers, recurrence, or additional global structure. Fused attention can avoid materializing the whole matrix; compute and communication still need accounting.
:::

### Exercise 4: A queue with misleading averages

Most rounds need $0.5\tau_c$ of service, but one in a thousand needs $100\tau_c$. Compute the mean service time. Does this establish that every feed-forward decision arrives within ten cycles?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

$\mathbb E S=0.999(0.5\tau_c)+0.001(100\tau_c)=0.5995\tau_c$, so average capacity can be sufficient. A rare hard round alone exceeds ten cycles and can create a backlog for later rounds. A tail-latency requirement needs a tail analysis, buffering, a bounded-time fallback, or a scheduling protocol that tolerates it.
:::
